evidence.title: Manzana de las Luces
evidence.snippet: Este bloque, rodeado de las calles Alsina, Moreno, Perú y Bolívar, es el hogar de muchos de los más importantes y tradicionales de educación, instituciones religiosas y culturales de Buenos Aires, que datan del siglo 17 y 18. El nombre de este bloque proviene del número de instituciones intelectuales que estaban presentes en los viejos tiempos. Una de las atracciones más interesantes es una red subterránea de túneles misteriosos que comunica cada edificio.

evidence.title: Mercado San Telmo
evidence.snippet: mercado alojado en una sala enorme Wrough-hierro. Todo, desde la albahaca fresca para zapatos y monedas antiguas se encuentra en exhibición en este mercado permanente. Venir durante la semana para ver el mercado de productos y la carne local. El domingo, cuando la acción está fuera, es prácticamente vacío.

evidence.title: Plaza Dorrego
evidence.snippet: La segunda plaza más antigua de Buenos Aires, seis días a la semana, la plaza es un espacio relativamente tranquilo, con sombra junto a restaurantes y cafés. Los domingos un mercado de antigüedades se hace cargo y casi no se puede ver la plaza del pueblo y puestos de mercado. Los puestos de ser anulado distancia de aproximadamente 17:00, y de 20:00 Hay baile público, incluyendo el tango.

San Telmo is the oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Steeped in colonial history, narrow cobblestone streets, and the soul of early tango, it offers a vivid look into the city's past.

evidence.title: 📜 Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.snippet: Origins (1580): Founded originally as Barrio Sur by Juan de Garay when he re-established Buenos Aires. It started as a humble industrial dockworker, brickmaking, and salting area along the river.
evidence.contextHeading: 📜 Brief History of San Telmo

evidence.title: 📜 Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.snippet: The Name: Named after San Pedro González Telmo, the patron saint of sailors, following the establishment of the Jesuits' Our Lady of Belén church.
evidence.contextHeading: 📜 Brief History of San Telmo

evidence.title: 📜 Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.snippet: The Yellow Fever Turning Point (1871): A devastating yellow fever epidemic forced wealthy elite families living in San Telmo to flee north to areas like Recoleta. Their grand colonial mansions were abandoned or converted into conventillos (multi-family tenement housing) for incoming waves of European immigrants.
evidence.contextHeading: 📜 Brief History of San Telmo

evidence.title: 📜 Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.snippet: Bohemian Revival: Decades later, the area transitioned into an artistic and bohemian hub, renowned today for preserving its 19th-century architecture, antique markets, and vibrant street culture.
evidence.contextHeading: 📜 Brief History of San Telmo

evidence.title: 🗺️ Itinerario para una Caminata Histórica (Key Stops on a Walking Tour)
evidence.source: 🗺️ Itinerario para una Caminata Histórica (Key Stops on a Walking Tour)
evidence.snippet: The beating heart of the neighborhood and the second-oldest public square in Buenos Aires. On Sundays, it transforms into the famous Feria de San Telmo antique market. Surrounding cafes make it the perfect place to stop and watch impromptu street tango.
evidence.contextHeading: 🗺️ Itinerario para una Caminata Histórica (Key Stops on a Walking Tour)

evidence.snippet: Located at Defensa 755, this is an incredible historical complex featuring subterranean brick tunnels and water streams dating back to the 1700s and 1800s. It offers a literal "underground layer" look at early Buenos Aires infrastructure.
evidence.contextHeading: 🗺️ Itinerario para una Caminata Histórica (Key Stops on a Walking Tour)

evidence.snippet: Built in 1897, this grand iron-and-timber indoor market retains its historic charm while functioning as a bustling food hall filled with local butchers, produce stands, cafes, and vintage stalls.
evidence.contextHeading: 🗺️ Itinerario para una Caminata Histórica (Key Stops on a Walking Tour)

evidence.title: 🗺️ Itinerario para una Caminata Histórica (Key Stops on a Walking Tour)
evidence.source: 🗺️ Itinerario para una Caminata Histórica (Key Stops on a Walking Tour)
evidence.snippet: A stunning example of a late-19th-century aristocratic mansion converted into a massive conventillo housing over 30 families. Today, it is restored and filled with antique and craft shops.
evidence.contextHeading: 🗺️ Itinerario para una Caminata Histórica (Key Stops on a Walking Tour)

evidence.snippet: Located at San Lorenzo 380, this is famously known as the narrowest house in Buenos Aires—measuring just 2.5 meters wide! Legend says it was freed or given to a freed slave, though historians debate the exact origin.
